# Median comparisons
![](images/median.png){style="width:400px; background:white; border-radius:5px" fig-align="center"}

MaAsLin3 analysis compares the coefficient of each feature against either 0 or the median coefficient value.
The median coefficient value being calculated from all the coefficient values of all the features for the one specific comparison (e.g. Rhizosphere Soil vs Bulk Soil).

Median comparison can be set in `maaslin3()` with the following 2 options:

- `median_comparison_abundance`: Median comparison for abundance/linear comparisons
    - By default is set to `TRUE`
- `median_comparison_prevalence`: Median comparison for prevalence/logistic comparisons
    - By default is set to `FALSE`

## Demonstration

Below is a quick example of how median and zero comparison differ.
In this case we'll compare Media (query) against Environment (reference).

### Count data

Say we have two groups: **Media** and **Environment**.
They'll each have one sample for simplicity. 
Below are the counts for 5 taxa:

|Taxa|Environment|Media|
|---|---|---|
|Taxon A | 100 | 200|
|Taxon B | 100 | 200|
|Taxon C | 100 | 200|
|Taxon D | 100 | 200|
|Taxon E | 100 | 400|

We can see that Taxa A-D each have 2 times the counts in the Media compared to the Environment, whilst Taxon E has 4 times.
As these are raw counts, the overall doubling could be due to library size, bacterial load, etc.

### Convert to relative abundance
In our [MaAsLin3 analysis](/maaslin3/maaslin3.qmd) we convert the counts to relative abundances (`normalization = 'TSS'`):

|Taxa|Environment|Media|
|---|---|---|
|Taxon A | 0.2 | 0.167|
|Taxon B | 0.2 | 0.167 |
|Taxon C | 0.2 | 0.167 |
|Taxon D | 0.2 | 0.167 |
|Taxon E | 0.2 | 0.333 |

Now it still appears like Taxon E has a higher count in Media but lower in the other taxa.

### Calculate coefficients (changes)

Next coefficients are calculated as log2-fold changes (coefficients explained in the [plots section](/maaslin3/plots.qmd)).

Feature|Relative abundance change| Coefficient|
|---|---|---|
|Taxon A | 0.167 / 0.2 | -0.26|
|Taxon B | 0.167 / 0.2 | -0.26 |
|Taxon C | 0.167 / 0.2 | -0.26 |
|Taxon D | 0.167 / 0.2 | -0.26 |
|Taxon E | 0.333 / 0.2 | 0.74 |

### Option 1: Compare to zero

Here we ask whether each feature’s coefficient is above or below **0**.

| Feature | Coefficient | Compared to zero | Simple interpretation |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Taxon A | -0.26 | < 0 | Appears decreased |
| Taxon B | -0.26 | < 0 | Appears decreased |
| Taxon C | -0.26 | < 0 | Appears decreased |
| Taxon D | -0.26 | < 0 | Appears decreased |
| Taxon E | 0.74 | > 0 | Appears increased |

When comparing the relative abundance coefficients to zero, Taxa A-D look like they are lower in the Media.

But we know from the raw counts that Taxa A-D were **not** lower in the Media. 
Their values were double compared to the Environment (100 to 200). 
They look lower because Taxon E was even higher, changing the relative composition of the sample.

### Option 2: Compare to the median coefficient

To compensate for this composition we can compare to the **median coefficient**.

For each comparison, in this case we only have one (Media vs Environment), a **median coefficient** is calculated.

The coefficients are:

`-0.26, -0.26, -0.26, -0.26, 0.74`

Therefore the **median coefficient** value is **-0.26**.
Instead of comparing each feature to **0**, we compare them to the **median coefficient**.

| Feature | Coefficient | Median coefficient | Compared to median | Simple interpretation |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| Taxon A | -0.26 | -0.26 | 0.00 | Typical/background change |
| Taxon B | -0.26 | -0.26 | 0.00 | Typical/background change |
| Taxon C | -0.26 | -0.26 | 0.00 | Typical/background change |
| Taxon D | -0.26 | -0.26 | 0.00 | Typical/background change |
| Taxon E | 0.74 | -0.26 | 1.00 | Increased more than typical |

### Conclusion

Comparing to **zero** makes the abundance of Taxa A-D look decreased in Media compared to the Environment. Comparing to the **median coefficient** does not treat Taxa A-D as specifically decreased. Instead, median comparison highlights Taxon E as the feature that changed more than the typical feature. So:

* Comparing to zero asks: *“Did this feature increase or decrease in relative abundance?"* 
* Comparing to the median asks: *"Did this feature change more or less than the typical feature”*

::: {.callout-important}
This is a simplified example with one sample per group. In a real MaAsLin3 analysis, the coefficients would come from a statistical model fitted across multiple samples, with uncertainty, p-values, and multiple-testing correction.
:::

## Abundance testing
![](images/abundance.png){style="width:150px; background:white; border-radius:5px; border: white solid 5px" fig-align="center"}

Median comparison is primarily used for abundance testing.
It accounts for compositionality and allows you to infer absolute scale changes when using relative abundance data (i.e. anything without absolute abundance values).

### Abundance median comparison

By default `median_comparison_abundance` is set to `TRUE`.
It should be used when using relative abundance values so you can make absolute scale inferences.
The primary reason for this is that testing against zero on the relative scale is not the same as testing against zero on the absolute scale.

When using abundance median comparison:

- A median coefficient for the comparison/metadatum (e.g. Rhizosphere Soil vs Bulk Soil) is created
- The abundance coefficient for each feature is tested against the median value 
- Compositionality is accounted for
- Only p-values and q-values change
- Coefficients in the results are the relative abundance coefficients unless `subtract_median = TRUE` is set

### Abundance zero comparison

When `median_comparison_abundance` is `FALSE` the coefficients are compared against 0.
This should be used when testing for:

- **Significant relative abundance** associations when using relative abundance data (i.e. you don't want to infer absolute scale changes)
- Absolute abundance associations under the assumption that the total absolute abundance is not changing
- Significant absolute abundance association when supplying spike-in with `unscaled_abundance`
- Significant absolute abundance association when supplying total abundance with `unscaled_abundance`

## Prevalence testing
![](images/prevalence.png){style="width:150px; background:white; border-radius:5px" fig-align="center"}

By default and for the vast majority of cases prevalence testing should be compared to 0 (`median_comparison_prevalence=FALSE`).

Median testing can be carried out when you are interested in determining if a specific prevalence association is significantly different to the median prevalence coefficient.
This won't be very often but it is an option.

## Median comparison threshold

When using either abundance or prevalence median comparison a threshold is set for each.
If the feature's coefficient is within threshold of the median its p-value will be set to 1.

For example:

- The median is 0.1
- The median threshold is 0.05
- Features with coefficient values from 0.05-0.15 will automatically have a p-value of 1

This prevents features which may have a statistical difference but not a substantially different value compared to the median from being detected as significant.

By default both `median_comparison_abundance_threshold` and `median_comparison_prevalence_threshold` are set to 0.
Therefore, only features whose coefficient match the median coefficient will automatically be given a p-value of 1.

## Conclusion
![](images/sum_ibm_magenta.png){style="width:150px; background:white; border-radius:5px; border: white 5px solid" fig-align="center"}

Our analysis is using a standard relative abundance dataset and we want to infer absolute scale changes. 
Therefore, we used the default parameters of `median_comparison_abundance=TRUE` and `median_comparison_prevalence=FALSE`.

More information and considerations can be found in the [MaAsLin3 manual](https://github.com/biobakery/Maaslin3#median-comparisons).
